why: Prices change by the hour and the shop; a static superlative is rot the day after it ships.
better: Compare the shop's own current menu, ask about same-day price rules, and call before driving.

why: Organic in cannabis has no single federal definition; the number inflates confidence without a source.
better: State which inputs, pest management, and soil practices the cultivator documents on the package or in their published notes.

why: Trust without a named source is a feeling, not evidence; readers can't tell what the claim rests on.
better: Name the source type (official page, shop page, direct note, third-party listing) and the date it was checked.

why: A medical recommendation implies endorsement from a clinician and a clinical context the page has not seen.
better: Refer readers to their own clinician for medical questions; describe product facts a label or shop can verify.

why: Cannabis in Maine is regulated as cannabis, not as a pharmaceutical; the label borrows authority the product does not carry.
better: Use the regulatory category the package actually lists and quote the test fields the lab report contains.

why: Solvent residue has established lab thresholds, not a 'cleanest' threshold; the superlative implies a measurement that does not exist.
better: Quote the residual-solvent panel from the certificate of analysis and the threshold the lab uses.

why: Method claims vary by cultivator; the same phrase on two labels can mean very different practices.
better: Point to the cultivator's published cultivation notes, the input list, and any third-party verification they share.

why: The phrase implies a clinical standard Maine dispensary cannabis is not packaged against; it muddles adult-use and medical programs.
better: Distinguish adult-use from medical product lines, list the program rules each one follows, and link to the current OCP source.

why: Natural is undefined in cannabis labeling; readers cannot tell which compounds, processes, or inputs the claim covers.
better: Replace with what the package lists: ingredients, cultivation inputs, and the specific process steps the cultivator publishes.

why: Quality without named criteria is a marketing container; every competitor can use the same word.
better: State the criteria a reader can actually check: batch details, package date, test results, and source notes.

why: Effect claims cross into outcome promises the page cannot stand behind for an individual reader.
better: Keep the copy to format, lineage, listed cannabinoids, and the questions a reader can ask at the counter.

why: Locally sourced without a geography or cultivator name is decorative; it tells the reader nothing they can verify.
better: Name the cultivator, the Maine town or region, and the license type the producer operates under.
